'''Gerald Stanford "Gerry" Guralnik''' ({{IPAc-en|g|ʊ|ˈ|r|æ|l|n|ɪ|k}}; September 17, 1936 – April 26, 2014) was the Chancellor’s Professor of [[Physics]] at [[Brown University]]. In 1964, he co-discovered the [[Higgs mechanism]] and [[Higgs boson]] with [[C. R. Hagen]] and [[Tom Kibble]] (GHK).<ref>

 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.13.585
 |doi-access=free
 }}</ref><ref>

 |s2cid=16298371

In 2010, Guralnik was awarded the [[American Physical Society]]'s [[Sakurai Prize|J. J. Sakurai Prize for Theoretical Particle Physics]] for the "elucidation of the properties of [[spontaneous symmetry breaking]] in four-dimensional relativistic [[gauge theory]] and of the mechanism for the consistent generation of [[vector boson]] masses".<ref>
{{cite web
 |url=http://www.aps.org/units/dpf/awards/recipient.cfm?first_nm=Gerald&last_nm=Guralnik&year=2010
 |title=2010 J.J. Sakurai Prize for Theoretical Particle Physics Recipient: Gerald S. Guralnik
 |publisher=[[American Physical Society]]
 |access-date=March 22, 2012
}}</ref>

Guralnik received his B.S. degree from the [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]] in 1958 and his Ph.D. degree from [[Harvard University]] in 1964.<ref>{{cite web
 |last=Luttrell
 |first=S. K.
 |date=March–April 2010
 |url=http://www.technologyreview.com/article/24610/
 |title=Gerald Guralnik '58 and Carl Richard Hagen '58, SM '58, PhD '63
 |work=[[Technology Review]]
 |access-date=March 22, 2012
 |archive-date=February 28, 2010
 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100228222713/http://www.technologyreview.com/article/24610/
 |url-status=dead
 }}</ref> He went to [[Imperial College London]] as a postdoctoral fellow supported by the [[National Science Foundation]] and then became a postdoctoral fellow at the [[University of Rochester]]. In the fall of 1967 Guralnik went to [[Brown University]] and frequently visited [[Imperial College London|Imperial College]] and [[Los Alamos National Laboratory]] where he was a staff member from 1985 to 1987. While at [[Los Alamos National Laboratory|Los Alamos]], he did extensive work on the development and application of computational methods for [[lattice QCD]]. 

Guralnik died of a heart attack at age 77 in 2014.<ref>{{Cite web |last1=April 28 |last2=Stacey 401-863-3766 |first2=2014 Media contact: Kevin |title=Gerald S. GuralnikChancellor's Professor of Physics |url=https://news.brown.edu/articles/2014/04/guralnik |access-date=2024-09-20 |website=news.brown.edu |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=After death, physics prof. remembered for mentorship, imagination and contributions to Nobel-winning work |url=https://www.browndailyherald.com/article/2014/05/after-death-physics-prof-remembered-for-mentorship-imagination-and-contributions-to-nobel-winning-work |access-date=2024-09-20 |website=The Brown Daily Herald |language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Hagen |first=Carl R. |date=2014-08-01 |title=Gerald Stanford Guralnik |url=https://pubs.aip.org/physicstoday/article/67/8/57/414784/Gerald-Stanford-Guralnik |journal=Physics Today |language=en |volume=67 |issue=8 |pages=57–58 |doi=10.1063/PT.3.2488 |issn=0031-9228}}</ref>
